One-Hit Wonders in Sports · 1988–2017

The one season that was the whole career.

Across 30 years and 8 pro leagues, 78 athletes had one elite season and never came close to repeating it. This is what their careers looked like.

Based on data from The Pudding 1,130 players · 14,982 player-seasons
Scroll
Two players, two spikes

The one season that was the whole career.

In 2005, Dontrelle Willis won 22 games for the Florida Marlins, pitched five shutouts, and finished second in NL Cy Young voting — the 8th-best player in baseball. Three years later, he was the 1,338th-best player in baseball. Two years after that, he was out of the majors for good.

Dana Barros did the same thing in basketball. In the 1994-95 season he averaged 20.6 points per game, made the All-Star team, won Most Improved Player, and finished 8th in the NBA in VORP. In the fourteen other seasons of his NBA career, he never once cracked the top 50 — his career-average rank was 153.

These are one-hit wonders, and they are not metaphors. They are what you get when you apply a strict statistical filter to thirty years of professional sports: athletes who were elite for one season and never came close again.

The definition

The rule that finds them.

The Pudding's 2018 analysis used two rules: one top-20 finish in your career, and no other top-50 finishes. Applied to 1,076 eligible careers across 8 leagues from 1988 to 2017, it identifies 78 one-hit wonders — 7.2% of all players who ever cracked the top 20 in their league. Roughly one in fourteen elite careers.

'Top 20' means something slightly different in each sport: basketball uses VORP (value above a replacement-level player), baseball uses WAR (wins above replacement), hockey uses point shares, golf uses money earned, tennis uses year-end ranking points. These were chosen because they're the closest thing each league has to a single number that answers 'who was most valuable this year.'

Statisticians have a name for the underlying phenomenon: regression to the mean. When any measurement mixes skill and luck — and a single season always does — the most extreme results are disproportionately luck-driven. Next year the skill remains, the luck resets, and the outlier drifts back toward the crowd. One-hit wonders are the extreme tail of that drift.

78 of 1,076 elite careers across 8 leagues had exactly one top-20 season and never came close again  ·  7.2%
By sport

Baseball is the one-hit wonder capital.

The rate of one-hit wonders is wildly uneven across sports. In Major League Baseball, 32 of 206 qualifying careers fit the strict definition — 15.5%, more than one in seven. The NHL is close behind at 13.0%, the PGA at 10.0%. Then a cliff: LPGA and NBA at 3.0%, ATP at 2.8%, WTA at 1.9%, and the WNBA at a single one-hit wonder across 120 careers — 0.8%.

Some of the gap is talent-pool size: MLB ranks hundreds more players than the NBA each year, so the ranks below 20 stretch much further down. Some is about the noisy single-number stats used in each sport: WAR and point shares swing year-to-year more than VORP does. Some is structural: the WNBA, the smallest league by historical data coverage, has compressed talent and a narrower top that players bounce around within.

However you explain it, the bottom line is that 'one-hit wonder' is primarily a baseball and hockey story. Half of all one-hit wonders in the dataset come from MLB alone.

They didn't peak at #1

They peaked at #17.

The stereotype of a one-hit wonder is a rookie sensation crashing from the very top. The data don't support it. Of the 78 one-hit wonders, only 4 (5%) peaked in the top 5 of their league. 15 peaked 6-10. 25 peaked 11-15. A full 34 — 44% of the total — peaked somewhere between rank 16 and 20. The typical one-hit wonder barely cleared the elite threshold.

Rank 17 was the single most common peak (9 players), followed by rank 19 (8) and rank 20 (7). Only three peaked at rank 4 — Alex Zhamnov (NHL, 1995), Darin Erstad (MLB, 2000), Mark Prior (MLB, 2003) — and exactly one at rank 5: Chase Headley, in 2012.

The right mental model is not 'MVP fell off a cliff.' It is 'rotational player had one honest All-Star season and went back to being a rotational player.'

When it happened

The peak usually came in year 4, 5, or 6.

And most one-hit wonders were not rookies at all. The peak season landed in career year 4-6 for 25 of 78 players (32%), and in year 7-10 for another 21 (27%). Only 9 had their best year as rookies. The median peak was a player's fifth season, with a standard deviation of 3.4 years.

They also weren't short-career players who flamed out. The 78 one-hit wonders played a mean of 12.5 seasons — only slightly shorter than the 13.3-season mean of other top-20 careers. Rich Beem played 20 seasons; Omar Vizquel played 24. One-hit wonders, on average, were not blink-and-you-miss-them. They were durable pros who spent a decade or more at journeyman level with one clean spike in the middle.

The fall

How far do they fall?

The gap between peak year and a one-hit wonder's typical season is the statistical signature of the phenomenon. The median one-hit wonder peaked at rank 15 and held a career-median rank near 200 — an 185-place gap. Within-sport, MLB one-hit wonders fall the furthest in relative terms: their median peak-to-typical spike is 22.9×. The LPGA sits at the other end with a 6.4× spike.

The fall is fast. Looking at the 75 players with an immediate next-year record, the median drop from peak to the very next season is 105 rank positions. MLB one-hit wonders dropped 132 places on average, NHL 118, LPGA 85, NBA 68, PGA 64. The median one-hit wonder was essentially not the same player one year later.

The canonical eight

Meet them — one per league.

The Pudding's 2018 article highlighted one poster-child per league. All eight still qualify when the strict definition is re-applied to the dataset. Dana Barros (NBA, peak rank 8 in 1995). Dontrelle Willis (MLB, peak 8 in 2005). Jiri Hudler (NHL, peak 13 in 2015). Rich Beem (PGA, peak 7 in 2002). Hilary Lunke (LPGA, peak 16 in 2003). Martin Verkerk (ATP, peak 19 in 2003). Karolina Sprem (WTA, peak 18 in 2004). Tracy Reid (WNBA, peak 15 in 1998).

Dana Barros's trajectory reads like a chart of a spike you can see from space: 191, 153, 125, 120, 92, 8, 98, 292, 103, 103, 295, 220, 368, DNP, 211. Six seasons of gradual climb, one season of stardom, eight seasons of reversion.

Dontrelle Willis's curve is sharper and shorter: 104, 109, 8, 127, 370, 1338, 1123, 1085, 399. Three years in the middle go from elite to last-man-in-the-majors, and everything after that is a long tail of minor-league comeback attempts.

Rich Beem's shape is the golf version — a money-driven spike. 1999 through 2002: $611K, $250K, $461K, $2.94M. Then: $1.01M, $230K, $701K, and a slow decline to $17K by 2016. One four-day PGA Championship over Tiger Woods restructured a career's earnings without restructuring the golfer.

The extreme tail

Baseball's biggest outliers.

Ranked by absolute gap between peak and career-median rank, the top of the list is almost entirely baseball. Andres Torres had the largest spike on record: rank 10 in the 2010 MLB on the championship-winning San Francisco Giants, a career-median rank of 848. Dave Hollins: rank 19 in 1992, median 719. Carlos Pena: rank 17 in 2007, median 481. These are not players who were close to elite every year — they were deep-roster professionals who had one season where everything clicked.

The only non-baseball players to crack the top 10 by this measure are Joachim Johansson (ATP, 2004, French Open semifinalist) and Pascal Dupuis (NHL, 2013, Penguins top line with Crosby). Sports with deeper talent pools and noisier metrics produce the most extreme individual outliers.

All 78

Browse them all.

All 78 one-hit wonders are listed in the table below, sortable by league, peak rank, or peak year. Browse and you'll find names familiar and unfamiliar: Jerry Stackhouse (NBA, once billed as 'the next Jordan'), Mark Prior (MLB rookie phenom, career ended by injury at 5 seasons), Ashleigh Barty (WTA, peaked at rank 17 in 2017 — and went on to become world #1 after this dataset ended).

Barty is the dataset's best reminder of its own limits. The data stop in 2017. Any player whose career was still accelerating at that point can look like a one-hit wonder in this snapshot and turn out, in reality, to be the opposite. Of our 78, most of the careers are fully closed — but a handful of 2015–2017 peakers are marked with an asterisk because their story may not be done.

Close

What the spike tells us.

The one-hit wonder has a statistical explanation — regression to the mean, applied to single-season metrics in leagues where the talent gradient is steep. It also has a human explanation, which the data cannot reach: a hot streak at the right moment, a perfect system fit, a coach or a teammate that made everything click, an injury that never healed the same way again, a young career that collapsed under the weight of expectation.

What the data show is that these careers are rare but not vanishingly so — 7% of elite careers — and they are distributed across the span of a career, not bunched at the front. The typical one-hit wonder was a professional for more than a decade and was good-but-not-great for most of it. One year, against probability, they were great. Then they weren't.

That's the shape worth remembering the next time someone has the best season of their career. It might be the beginning of something. Or it might be exactly what it looks like.
